headline: Plague lab worker in Russia dies of pneumonia

sources.title: Russia reports a worker at a Siberian plague institute got pneumonia from an unknown cause and died (AP, via KTRE)
Russian lab worker dies of suspected plague as 200 enter medical observation (NBC News)
Russian lab worker dies of suspected plague in Siberia; US monitoring case (Al Jazeera)
What to know about pneumonic plague after Russian lab worker's death (video, PBS NewsHour)

chunks.text: A worker at a plague [[research institute]] in eastern Russia has died, and Russian officials say the cause is unknown. The 28-year-old [[laboratory technician]] {{came down with}} [[pneumonia]] and died last week in a local hospital. [[Unconfirmed]] media reports said she may have had pneumonic plague. This rare form can be {{passed on}} from person to person. Her death has {{set off}} fears in Russia and abroad.

verbs.correct: To become sick with an illness
verbs.wrong: To study a disease in a lab
verbs.why: I think I'm coming down with the flu. My son came down with a cold after the trip. The 28-year-old laboratory technician came down with pneumonia and died last week.

verbs.correct: To spread a disease to another person
verbs.wrong: To be cured quickly with medicine
verbs.why: Cover your mouth so you don't pass on your cold. Kids at day care pass on colds all the time. Pneumonic plague is a rare form of plague that can be passed on from person to person.

verbs.wrong: To delay the work of a lab
verbs.why: The news set off panic at the grocery store. Her comment set off anger online. The worker's death has set off fears in Russia and abroad.

chunks.text: The hospital was put under [[quarantine]] on Friday, October 2. It stopped {{taking in}} new patients. Its laboratory also stopped {{carrying out}} [[routine tests]]. About 200 people who may have had contact with her are under [[medical observation]], according to regional officials. Tests on her contacts {{turned up}} two cases of a [[common cold]] virus and two cases of the coronavirus. The director of a nearby [[aluminum plant]] told workers to wear masks.

verbs.wrong: To hire new nurses and doctors
verbs.why: The emergency room is too busy to take in more patients. The hospital took in many people after the crash. The hospital in quarantine stopped taking in new patients.

verbs.correct: To do or complete a task
verbs.why: Our team carries out a safety check every week. The nurse carried out the blood test quickly. The hospital's laboratory stopped carrying out routine tests.

verbs.wrong: To cost the hospital a lot of money
verbs.why: My search turned up an old photo of my grandparents. The inspection turned up a problem with the wiring. Tests on the woman's contacts turned up two cases of a common cold virus and two cases of the coronavirus.

chunks.text: Russia's health agency has {{looked into}} the case. On Sunday, it said the woman had pneumonia of [[unknown origin]]. It said [[extensive]] testing found no germs linked to her work. The leader of a neighboring region said she died "maybe of the plague." He also said no disease had {{broken out}} in his region. A former head of the health agency said it was most likely not plague. A Kremlin spokesman {{played down}} the [[rumors]]. He told people to trust [[official statements]] instead.

verbs.correct: To study something to learn the facts
verbs.wrong: To give medicine to a patient
verbs.why: The manager is looking into the problem. Police looked into the missing money. Russia's health agency has looked into the case and found no germs linked to her work.

verbs.wrong: To be named after a place
verbs.why: A fire broke out in the old factory. The flu broke out at the nursing home. The leader of a neighboring region said no disease had broken out there.

verbs.correct: To make something seem less important
verbs.wrong: To pretend you share an opinion
verbs.why: The coach played down the team's loss. The mayor played down the problem with the buses. A Kremlin spokesman played down the rumors and told people to trust official statements.

chunks.text: The World Health Organization said no cause of death has been officially confirmed. On Monday, the US secretary of state said the case was not a [[cause for alarm]]. He said the US is [[monitoring]] it closely. The State Department {{called on}} Russia to share [[accurate information]] quickly and openly. One British expert {{pointed out}} that plague still exists in many parts of the world. [[Antibiotics]] can treat it if it is caught early, experts say.

verbs.correct: To formally ask someone to do something
verbs.wrong: To cancel a planned meeting or trip
verbs.why: Teachers called on the state to raise their pay. The mayor called on drivers to use less gas. The State Department called on Russia to share accurate information quickly and openly.

verbs.correct: To mention a fact people should notice
verbs.wrong: To choose one thing from a group
verbs.why: My friend pointed out that the bus was late again. The doctor pointed out that I need more sleep. One British expert pointed out that plague still exists in many parts of the world.

mainIdea.s: A young technician at a plague lab in eastern Russia died of pneumonia, and about 200 people are being watched. Officials say the cause is unknown, and plague is not confirmed.
mainIdea.why: Russia's health agency said she had pneumonia of unknown origin. About 200 contacts are under medical observation, and no one has officially confirmed plague.

mainIdea.s: Russian health officials have confirmed that a lab worker died of plague. Her hospital is now closed, and the United States has warned that the disease is spreading fast.
mainIdea.why: Close, but no one has officially confirmed plague. Russia's health agency said the cause is unknown, and the US said the case was not a cause for alarm.

mainIdea.s: Russia has opened a new research center in the far east to study old diseases like plague. Scientists there will train young doctors and share their work with other countries.
mainIdea.why: A lab worker died of pneumonia of unknown origin. Officials are still checking whether plague played any part.

lines.text: Did you see the news about the plague lab worker in Russia?
I saw a headline. What happened?
A young lab technician {{came down with}} pneumonia and died last week. She worked at a plague research institute in eastern Russia.
Nobody knows yet. Some media reports say it was, but nothing has been confirmed.
That kind of plague can be {{passed on}} between people, right? That must have {{set off}} a lot of fears.
It did. The hospital stopped {{taking in}} new patients, and about 200 people are under medical observation.
Two hundred people? That sounds like a lot.
It's done [[out of an abundance of caution]]. Tests on her contacts {{turned up}} a couple of colds and two coronavirus cases, but nothing more.
The health agency {{looked into}} it and found no germs linked to her job. A Kremlin spokesman {{played down}} the reports.
I bet the [[rumor mill]] is busy, though.
Probably. People nearby must be [[on edge]]. A local aluminum plant even told workers to wear masks.
Is the rest of the world worried?
The US says it's watching closely, but it sees no cause for alarm. It {{called on}} Russia to share information quickly and openly.
Good. In a [[health scare]] like this, people need clear facts.
[[For the record]], experts {{point out}} that antibiotics can treat plague if it's caught early.
Well, that helps. I hope the tests give a clear answer soon.

expressions.expr: out of an abundance of caution
expressions.def: Used to say something is done to be extra safe, not because of a known danger
ex: The school closed early out of an abundance of caution.
Out of an abundance of caution, the airline checked every plane.

expressions.def: People spreading stories that may not be true
ex: The rumor mill says our boss is leaving.
Don't trust the rumor mill at work.

expressions.def: Nervous and worried about what might happen
ex: Everyone was on edge while we waited for the test results.

expressions.def: A time when people fear a disease, often before the facts are clear
ex: The health scare kept many families at home.
After the health scare, he started eating better.

expressions.def: Used to state a fact clearly so people remember it
ex: For the record, I never said that.
For the record, the meeting starts at nine.
